# The Irish Athletics Podcast: Second-generation marathon runner Aoife Talty follows in her Mam’s footsteps - Athletics Ireland
## The Irish Athletics Podcast: Second-generation marathon runner Aoife Talty follows in her Mam’s footsteps
“I did hear a lot of people kind of saying you lose yourself in motherhood. I never lost myself in motherhood. I kind of just fully surrendered to it the first time because it’s totally new.
“You’re doing a total new job. Every second of the day, you’re kind of wondering what I should do next. You’re learning, you’re reading, you’re listening to podcasts.
“And there just wasn’t space in my head, in my mind to think about running.”
Aoife Talty pictured in 2013 when Raheny Shamrock were team winners at the Inter Club Cross Country Championships
The 40-year-old was a talented runner in her youth, and has been a proud member of Raheny Shamrock since she first started running, but due to recurring injuries, hadn’t run consistently in the ten years before starting her marathon block.
When her second daughter, Grace was born, the recovery was easier and thoughts soon turned to a possible return to running.
“The recovery for me was night and day between my first delivery and my second delivery. So I recovered really well.
“I actually felt as I was leaving the hospital that I was nearly recovered. So that was October. And so the back of my head, I was thinking, could I run the marathon next year? Is it too soon? Like bearing in mind that I hadn’t run in 10 years.”
There have been many changes in the running world over the last 40 years, meaning the experiences of the two generations have been different. Shoes, nutrition, training and technology have all become more advanced.
Márie ran an impressive best of three hours and 35 minutes without the bells and whistles that Aoife has been afforded, and saw her clock an impressive three hours and nine minutes for the 26.2 distance on her first attempt.
“Her best time was 3.35. That she could run those times with no super shoes. I think we’re all getting caught up with the technology and the, you know, the super shoes and the fuelling… but I’d be so interested to see what kind of time she could have run if she had all the things that I have.”

# The Irish Athletics Podcast: Second-generation marathon runner Aoife Talty follows in her Mam’s footsteps - Athletics Ireland
## The Irish Athletics Podcast: Second-generation marathon runner Aoife Talty follows in her Mam’s footsteps
One similarity of the experience of mother and daughter that Talty highlights is the support of their families.
“I suppose the similarities there are that she had- My dad was really supportive as well, it was probably out of season for him. His GAA was over. So it was her time to go out and run.
“I never remember as a child thinking, where’s mam going? Or missing mam when she was going training. The memories that I have are just wanting to be like her.
“I never remember thinking, ‘Where is she? She should be here’. Maybe there was judgement from other people. I don’t know that. But for us, we were four very happy kids thinking how amazing our mom was. That’s the memory that I have.”
Aoife Talty represented Ireland at the Rás na hÉireann 2011 but didn't compete for ten years before having her children

**Brian Gerard O'Driscoll** (born 21 January 1979) is an Irish former professional rugby union player. He played his entire career at outside centre for the Irish provincial team Leinster and for Ireland. He captained Ireland from 2003 until 2012, and captained the British & Irish Lions for their 2005 tour of New Zealand. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest rugby players of all time.

O'Driscoll is the sixth most-capped player in rugby union history, having played 141 test matches: 133 for Ireland (83 as captain), and 8 for the Lions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-PROFILE-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-espnscrum-2) With 46 tries for Ireland and 1 try for the Lions in 2001, he is Ireland's highest-ever try scorer;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-PROFILE-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-3) additionally, he is the 10th-highest try scorer in international rugby union history and the highest-scoring centre of all time. He also holds the record for the most Six Nations tries with 26.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-smh-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-indep-5) O'Driscoll was chosen as Player of the Tournament in the 2006, 2007 and 2009 Six Nations Championships.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-guardian-6)

He was inducted into the World Rugby Hall of Fame on 17 November 2016 at the opening ceremony of its first location in Rugby, England.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-7) Since retirement, he has worked as a pundit and analyst for BT Sport and ITV Sport and ventured into business start-ups, including the Ultimate Rugby mobile app[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-8) and Zipp, an Irish e-scooter business.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-9) O'Driscoll was involved in Irish Rugby's unsuccessful bid to host the 2023 World Cup.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-10)

O'Driscoll was born and bred in Clontarf in the northside of Dublin to [Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_O'Driscoll "Frank O'Driscoll") and Geraldine O'Driscoll, both physicians. He had barely played rugby until he went to the rugby nursery Blackrock College, from the age of 12.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-12) O'Driscoll's family was steeped in rugby. His father, Frank, played two games for Ireland[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-13) and a cousin of his father, [Barry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_O'Driscoll "Barry O'Driscoll"), won four caps.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-:0-14) Another cousin of Frank's, Barry's brother [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_O'Driscoll_(rugby_union) "John O'Driscoll (rugby union)"), represented Ireland 26 times and was a member of the Lions teams that toured South Africa in 1980 and New Zealand in 1983.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-:0-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-:1-15)
As a child, O'Driscoll played Gaelic football before switching to rugby.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-Profile-16) For his secondary education, he attended Blackrock College, where he played in the Leinster Senior Cup team in 1996 and 1997.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-Profile-16)

Although O'Driscoll started the first two rounds of the competition in 1996, he was subsequently dropped to the bench for the remainder of the competition, and was an unused replacement in the team's victorious final appearance. In 1997 they were beaten in the quarter-final by Clongowes.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-17) He was capped three times for Ireland Schools in 1996.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-ieProfile-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-LeinProfile-19)
In 1998, O'Driscoll played for the Ireland U-19 side, which won the Under 19 Rugby World Championship.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-20)
After leaving school, he attended University College Dublin (UCD) on a scholarship and graduated with a Diploma in Sports Management in 1998.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-BOD-22)
While at UCD, he first made the under-20 side, before being promoted to the top team near the end of his first year.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-BOD-22) O'Driscoll made his Ireland under-21 debut in February 1999, and eventually gained four caps.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-LeinProfile-19)
In 2009, he received the UCD Foundation Day Medal for his sporting achievements.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-23)

O'Driscoll made his debut for Leinster in 1999, and under head coach Matt Williams and backs coach Alan Gaffney he became an explosive force in the Leinster backline, forming a highly effective centre partnership with Shane Horgan. In 2001, Leinster won the inaugural Celtic League beating Munster in Lansdowne Road. In 2003, Leinster were heavy favourites for that year's Heineken Cup but were beaten by Perpignan in the semi-finals.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-BBC-24)
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brian_O'Driscoll_Leinster.jpg)
O'Driscoll on 10 November 2007. Leinster Rugby v Leicester Tigers in Heineken Cup
Leinster appointed Michael Cheika in the summer of 2005 and despite rumours of O'Driscoll moving to France, O'Driscoll agreed to another year in Ireland. That year, O'Driscoll returning from a shoulder injury suffered on the Lions tour, would assume the captaincy for the season. Under backs coach David Knox and the movement of Argentine international Felipe Contepomi to fly half, the Leinster backline became one of the most potent in Europe.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-25)
O'Driscoll excelled in wins over Bath Rugby and Toulouse away from home. These victories would set up a Heineken Cup semi-final in Lansdowne Road against Munster, but defeat against the eventual champions Munster would deny O'Driscoll and his team a final berth. Leinster were also denied a Magners League title, with David Humphreys of Ulster slotting an injury-time drop goal to give victory to Ulster in their final game of the season.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-26)

In 2007, Wasps beat Leinster in the quarter-finals of the Heineken Cup. In 2008, Leinster lost in the group stages. In 2007, Leinster reached the final hurdle of the Magners league only to be denied by the Ospreys and Cardiff. In 2008, Leinster won that title ahead of Munster, marking O'Driscoll's second honour with the province, his first and only as captain._[citation needed_]
The 2008–09 season marked a shift in focus for O'Driscoll. While retaining the Irish captaincy under new coach Declan Kidney, he handed the honour of Leinster captain to Leo Cullen. O'Driscoll scored two tries in the defeat of English champions London Wasps, however, this victory was followed by away defeats for Leinster to both London Wasps and Castres. Leinster advanced to the quarter-finals to face [Harlequins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlequin_F.C. "Harlequin F.C.") at the Twickenham Stoop. When O'Driscoll was absent through injury in April 2009, Leinster relinquished their Magners League crown to Munster at Thomond Park. Against Harlequins, Leinster scored a 6–5 victory, the game infamous for the Bloodgate incident.
In the semi-final against rivals Munster in Croke Park, an 82,206 sell-out, O'Driscoll was awarded the man of the match award (which he later dedicated to the entire team) after an intercept try completed a convincing win for Leinster and sent O'Driscoll to his first Heineken Cup final.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-27) Leinster captured the Heineken Cup against Leicester Tigers on 23 May 2009. The 19–16 Heineken Cup victory included a drop goal from O'Driscoll who was suffering from a shoulder injury.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-28)

**Brian Gerard O'Driscoll** (born 21 January 1979) is an Irish former professional rugby union player. He played his entire career at outside centre for the Irish provincial team Leinster and for Ireland. He captained Ireland from 2003 until 2012, and captained the British & Irish Lions for their 2005 tour of New Zealand. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest rugby players of all time.
texts.2: O'Driscoll is the sixth most-capped player in rugby union history, having played 141 test matches: 133 for Ireland (83 as captain), and 8 for the Lions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-PROFILE-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-espnscrum-2) With 46 tries for Ireland and 1 try for the Lions in 2001, he is Ireland's highest-ever try scorer;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-PROFILE-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-3) additionally, he is the 10th-highest try scorer in international rugby union history and the highest-scoring centre of all time. He also holds the record for the most Six Nations tries with 26.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-smh-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-indep-5) O'Driscoll was chosen as Player of the Tournament in the 2006, 2007 and 2009 Six Nations Championships.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-guardian-6)
texts.3: He was inducted into the World Rugby Hall of Fame on 17 November 2016 at the opening ceremony of its first location in Rugby, England.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-7) Since retirement, he has worked as a pundit and analyst for BT Sport and ITV Sport and ventured into business start-ups, including the Ultimate Rugby mobile app[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-8) and Zipp, an Irish e-scooter business.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-9) O'Driscoll was involved in Irish Rugby's unsuccessful bid to host the 2023 World Cup.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-10)

# The Irish Athletics Podcast: Second-generation marathon runner Aoife Talty follows in her Mam’s footsteps - Athletics Ireland
## The Irish Athletics Podcast: Second-generation marathon runner Aoife Talty follows in her Mam’s footsteps
“I did hear a lot of people kind of saying you lose yourself in motherhood. I never lost myself in motherhood. I kind of just fully surrendered to it the first time because it’s totally new.
“You’re doing a total new job. Every second of the day, you’re kind of wondering what I should do next. You’re learning, you’re reading, you’re listening to podcasts.
“And there just wasn’t space in my head, in my mind to think about running.”
Aoife Talty pictured in 2013 when Raheny Shamrock were team winners at the Inter Club Cross Country Championships
The 40-year-old was a talented runner in her youth, and has been a proud member of Raheny Shamrock since she first started running, but due to recurring injuries, hadn’t run consistently in the ten years before starting her marathon block.
When her second daughter, Grace was born, the recovery was easier and thoughts soon turned to a possible return to running.
“The recovery for me was night and day between my first delivery and my second delivery. So I recovered really well.
“I actually felt as I was leaving the hospital that I was nearly recovered. So that was October. And so the back of my head, I was thinking, could I run the marathon next year? Is it too soon? Like bearing in mind that I hadn’t run in 10 years.”
There have been many changes in the running world over the last 40 years, meaning the experiences of the two generations have been different. Shoes, nutrition, training and technology have all become more advanced.
Márie ran an impressive best of three hours and 35 minutes without the bells and whistles that Aoife has been afforded, and saw her clock an impressive three hours and nine minutes for the 26.2 distance on her first attempt.
“Her best time was 3.35. That she could run those times with no super shoes. I think we’re all getting caught up with the technology and the, you know, the super shoes and the fuelling… but I’d be so interested to see what kind of time she could have run if she had all the things that I have.”

# The Irish Athletics Podcast: Second-generation marathon runner Aoife Talty follows in her Mam’s footsteps - Athletics Ireland
## The Irish Athletics Podcast: Second-generation marathon runner Aoife Talty follows in her Mam’s footsteps
One similarity of the experience of mother and daughter that Talty highlights is the support of their families.
“I suppose the similarities there are that she had- My dad was really supportive as well, it was probably out of season for him. His GAA was over. So it was her time to go out and run.
“I never remember as a child thinking, where’s mam going? Or missing mam when she was going training. The memories that I have are just wanting to be like her.
“I never remember thinking, ‘Where is she? She should be here’. Maybe there was judgement from other people. I don’t know that. But for us, we were four very happy kids thinking how amazing our mom was. That’s the memory that I have.”
Aoife Talty represented Ireland at the Rás na hÉireann 2011 but didn't compete for ten years before having her children

**Brian Gerard O'Driscoll** (born 21 January 1979) is an Irish former professional rugby union player. He played his entire career at outside centre for the Irish provincial team Leinster and for Ireland. He captained Ireland from 2003 until 2012, and captained the British & Irish Lions for their 2005 tour of New Zealand. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest rugby players of all time.

O'Driscoll is the sixth most-capped player in rugby union history, having played 141 test matches: 133 for Ireland (83 as captain), and 8 for the Lions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-PROFILE-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-espnscrum-2) With 46 tries for Ireland and 1 try for the Lions in 2001, he is Ireland's highest-ever try scorer;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-PROFILE-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-3) additionally, he is the 10th-highest try scorer in international rugby union history and the highest-scoring centre of all time. He also holds the record for the most Six Nations tries with 26.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-smh-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-indep-5) O'Driscoll was chosen as Player of the Tournament in the 2006, 2007 and 2009 Six Nations Championships.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-guardian-6)

He was inducted into the World Rugby Hall of Fame on 17 November 2016 at the opening ceremony of its first location in Rugby, England.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-7) Since retirement, he has worked as a pundit and analyst for BT Sport and ITV Sport and ventured into business start-ups, including the Ultimate Rugby mobile app[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-8) and Zipp, an Irish e-scooter business.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-9) O'Driscoll was involved in Irish Rugby's unsuccessful bid to host the 2023 World Cup.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-10)

O'Driscoll was born and bred in Clontarf in the northside of Dublin to [Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_O'Driscoll "Frank O'Driscoll") and Geraldine O'Driscoll, both physicians. He had barely played rugby until he went to the rugby nursery Blackrock College, from the age of 12.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-12) O'Driscoll's family was steeped in rugby. His father, Frank, played two games for Ireland[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-13) and a cousin of his father, [Barry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_O'Driscoll "Barry O'Driscoll"), won four caps.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-:0-14) Another cousin of Frank's, Barry's brother [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_O'Driscoll_(rugby_union) "John O'Driscoll (rugby union)"), represented Ireland 26 times and was a member of the Lions teams that toured South Africa in 1980 and New Zealand in 1983.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-:0-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-:1-15)
As a child, O'Driscoll played Gaelic football before switching to rugby.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-Profile-16) For his secondary education, he attended Blackrock College, where he played in the Leinster Senior Cup team in 1996 and 1997.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-Profile-16)

Although O'Driscoll started the first two rounds of the competition in 1996, he was subsequently dropped to the bench for the remainder of the competition, and was an unused replacement in the team's victorious final appearance. In 1997 they were beaten in the quarter-final by Clongowes.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-17) He was capped three times for Ireland Schools in 1996.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-ieProfile-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-LeinProfile-19)
In 1998, O'Driscoll played for the Ireland U-19 side, which won the Under 19 Rugby World Championship.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-20)
After leaving school, he attended University College Dublin (UCD) on a scholarship and graduated with a Diploma in Sports Management in 1998.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-BOD-22)
While at UCD, he first made the under-20 side, before being promoted to the top team near the end of his first year.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-BOD-22) O'Driscoll made his Ireland under-21 debut in February 1999, and eventually gained four caps.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-LeinProfile-19)
In 2009, he received the UCD Foundation Day Medal for his sporting achievements.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-23)

O'Driscoll made his debut for Leinster in 1999, and under head coach Matt Williams and backs coach Alan Gaffney he became an explosive force in the Leinster backline, forming a highly effective centre partnership with Shane Horgan. In 2001, Leinster won the inaugural Celtic League beating Munster in Lansdowne Road. In 2003, Leinster were heavy favourites for that year's Heineken Cup but were beaten by Perpignan in the semi-finals.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-BBC-24)
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brian_O'Driscoll_Leinster.jpg)
O'Driscoll on 10 November 2007. Leinster Rugby v Leicester Tigers in Heineken Cup
Leinster appointed Michael Cheika in the summer of 2005 and despite rumours of O'Driscoll moving to France, O'Driscoll agreed to another year in Ireland. That year, O'Driscoll returning from a shoulder injury suffered on the Lions tour, would assume the captaincy for the season. Under backs coach David Knox and the movement of Argentine international Felipe Contepomi to fly half, the Leinster backline became one of the most potent in Europe.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-25)
O'Driscoll excelled in wins over Bath Rugby and Toulouse away from home. These victories would set up a Heineken Cup semi-final in Lansdowne Road against Munster, but defeat against the eventual champions Munster would deny O'Driscoll and his team a final berth. Leinster were also denied a Magners League title, with David Humphreys of Ulster slotting an injury-time drop goal to give victory to Ulster in their final game of the season.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-26)

In 2007, Wasps beat Leinster in the quarter-finals of the Heineken Cup. In 2008, Leinster lost in the group stages. In 2007, Leinster reached the final hurdle of the Magners league only to be denied by the Ospreys and Cardiff. In 2008, Leinster won that title ahead of Munster, marking O'Driscoll's second honour with the province, his first and only as captain._[citation needed_]
The 2008–09 season marked a shift in focus for O'Driscoll. While retaining the Irish captaincy under new coach Declan Kidney, he handed the honour of Leinster captain to Leo Cullen. O'Driscoll scored two tries in the defeat of English champions London Wasps, however, this victory was followed by away defeats for Leinster to both London Wasps and Castres. Leinster advanced to the quarter-finals to face [Harlequins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlequin_F.C. "Harlequin F.C.") at the Twickenham Stoop. When O'Driscoll was absent through injury in April 2009, Leinster relinquished their Magners League crown to Munster at Thomond Park. Against Harlequins, Leinster scored a 6–5 victory, the game infamous for the Bloodgate incident.
In the semi-final against rivals Munster in Croke Park, an 82,206 sell-out, O'Driscoll was awarded the man of the match award (which he later dedicated to the entire team) after an intercept try completed a convincing win for Leinster and sent O'Driscoll to his first Heineken Cup final.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-27) Leinster captured the Heineken Cup against Leicester Tigers on 23 May 2009. The 19–16 Heineken Cup victory included a drop goal from O'Driscoll who was suffering from a shoulder injury.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll#cite_note-28)

# The Irish Athletics Podcast: Second-generation marathon runner Aoife Talty follows in her Mam’s footsteps - Athletics Ireland
## The Irish Athletics Podcast: Second-generation marathon runner Aoife Talty follows in her Mam’s footsteps
“I did hear a lot of people kind of saying you lose yourself in motherhood. I never lost myself in motherhood. I kind of just fully surrendered to it the first time because it’s totally new.
“You’re doing a total new job. Every second of the day, you’re kind of wondering what I should do next. You’re learning, you’re reading, you’re listening to podcasts.
“And there just wasn’t space in my head, in my mind to think about running.”
Aoife Talty pictured in 2013 when Raheny Shamrock were team winners at the Inter Club Cross Country Championships
The 40-year-old was a talented runner in her youth, and has been a proud member of Raheny Shamrock since she first started running, but due to recurring injuries, hadn’t run consistently in the ten years before starting her marathon block.
When her second daughter, Grace was born, the recovery was easier and thoughts soon turned to a possible return to running.
“The recovery for me was night and day between my first delivery and my second delivery. So I recovered really well.
“I actually felt as I was leaving the hospital that I was nearly recovered. So that was October. And so the back of my head, I was thinking, could I run the marathon next year? Is it too soon? Like bearing in mind that I hadn’t run in 10 years.”
There have been many changes in the running world over the last 40 years, meaning the experiences of the two generations have been different. Shoes, nutrition, training and technology have all become more advanced.
Márie ran an impressive best of three hours and 35 minutes without the bells and whistles that Aoife has been afforded, and saw her clock an impressive three hours and nine minutes for the 26.2 distance on her first attempt.
“Her best time was 3.35. That she could run those times with no super shoes. I think we’re all getting caught up with the technology and the, you know, the super shoes and the fuelling… but I’d be so interested to see what kind of time she could have run if she had all the things that I have.”

# The Irish Athletics Podcast: Second-generation marathon runner Aoife Talty follows in her Mam’s footsteps - Athletics Ireland
## The Irish Athletics Podcast: Second-generation marathon runner Aoife Talty follows in her Mam’s footsteps
One similarity of the experience of mother and daughter that Talty highlights is the support of their families.
“I suppose the similarities there are that she had- My dad was really supportive as well, it was probably out of season for him. His GAA was over. So it was her time to go out and run.
“I never remember as a child thinking, where’s mam going? Or missing mam when she was going training. The memories that I have are just wanting to be like her.
“I never remember thinking, ‘Where is she? She should be here’. Maybe there was judgement from other people. I don’t know that. But for us, we were four very happy kids thinking how amazing our mom was. That’s the memory that I have.”
Aoife Talty represented Ireland at the Rás na hÉireann 2011 but didn't compete for ten years before having her children

# Dooney Family Join Prestigious List - Athletics Ireland
## Dooney Family Join Prestigious List
#### Dooney Family Become the 13th Father and Son to be Capped for Ireland at Senior Level
*Information compiled by Pierce O’Callaghan
Following on from Tuesday’s announcement that Conor Dooney (Raheny Shamrock AC) will now represent Ireland at the European Cross Country Championships in Bulgaria, the Dooney family have made a bit of history of their own. Conor’s father Roy Dooney was capped 19 times for Ireland at senior level. Together they become the 13th father and son to be capped for Ireland at senior level since 1876. Making it a real family affair younger brother Kevin will also be in the team representing Ireland in the U23 race in Bulgaria.

# Dooney Family Join Prestigious List - Athletics Ireland
## Dooney Family Join Prestigious List
#### Previous Father and Son Caps
The previous time this happened was earlier in the year with Eamon and John Coghlan when John gained his first cap at the Penn Relays in April. They join current father & son combinations of Tim & Timmy Crowe, Brendan & Shane Quinn, Paul & Colin Quirke.
Sara Treacy is the daughter of Siobhan Lonergan who was capped four times for Ireland at senior level. Linked to this is the mother & son combination of Patricia Amond & Marcus Lawler and the father, mother and daughter combination of Brian McManus, Mary McManus (nee McKenna) and their daughter Catherine who won her first cap at the European Team Championships in June 2014. In addition to this the father & daughter combination of Mark & Katie Kirk who became the first father & daughter to win Irish senior titles since the championships began in 1873.

# Dooney Family Join Prestigious List - Athletics Ireland
## Dooney Family Join Prestigious List
#### Dooney Family Become the 13th Father and Son to be Capped for Ireland at Senior Level
*Information compiled by Pierce O’Callaghan
Following on from Tuesday’s announcement that Conor Dooney (Raheny Shamrock AC) will now represent Ireland at the European Cross Country Championships in Bulgaria, the Dooney family have made a bit of history of their own. Conor’s father Roy Dooney was capped 19 times for Ireland at senior level. Together they become the 13th father and son to be capped for Ireland at senior level since 1876. Making it a real family affair younger brother Kevin will also be in the team representing Ireland in the U23 race in Bulgaria.

# Dooney Family Join Prestigious List - Athletics Ireland
## Dooney Family Join Prestigious List
#### Previous Father and Son Caps
The previous time this happened was earlier in the year with Eamon and John Coghlan when John gained his first cap at the Penn Relays in April. They join current father & son combinations of Tim & Timmy Crowe, Brendan & Shane Quinn, Paul & Colin Quirke.
Sara Treacy is the daughter of Siobhan Lonergan who was capped four times for Ireland at senior level. Linked to this is the mother & son combination of Patricia Amond & Marcus Lawler and the father, mother and daughter combination of Brian McManus, Mary McManus (nee McKenna) and their daughter Catherine who won her first cap at the European Team Championships in June 2014. In addition to this the father & daughter combination of Mark & Katie Kirk who became the first father & daughter to win Irish senior titles since the championships began in 1873.

Title: Celtic/DCH Athletics Club on Instagram: "It is with a heavy heart that we share the news of the passing of our esteemed club coach, stalwart, and friend, Brian McManus, who was laid to rest last week. 

Brian leaves behind an extraordinary legacy within the athletics community, beautifully captured in this tribute by Dermot Nagle on behalf of the members of Dublin City Harriers and Celtic DCH last week:

“We are heartbroken saying goodbye to our esteemed club member, Brian McManus.

It’s probably a little known fact but Brian was the grandson of the legendary Donore Harrier, Charlie McManus. Athletics was in his blood but it was Dublin City Harriers which he joined to hone his sprinting skills, which were considerable.

He quickly established himself as an accomplished athlete and was a member of some great DCH teams of the 1970s and 1980’s. Brian was an international athlete at both junior and senior levels at 400m and 4 x 400m, in which he recorded sub 48 secs, more than 40 years ago.

Following retirement Brian was involved in administration and was club secretary for a period. It was really coaching which he preferred and over time he put together a strong group of athletes who achieved much. All of Brian’s considerable talents were available to and used by DCH. His quiet, modest, and relaxed approach hid a steely determination to achieve pre-set aims and ambitions.

Above all Brian was a family man; he adored Mary and his daughters Susan and Catherine all of whom were international athletes and represented our country with distinction.

Tomorrow, young and old, we will form a tearful guard of honour at the church. We will mourn and miss this fabulous man, our colleague, our clubmate and our friend who was taken from us too soon, far too soon”.

Rest in peace, Brian. You will be deeply and sadly missed, but your legacy will live on in every lap we run."

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Gerard O’Donnell from Carrick on Shannon AC coached by Jeremy Lyons and Aideen Sinnott.
The Athletics Ireland RDO is back in action for the 2022 season, the limited competitive season in 2021 seen him still have a very strong performance coming first in the 60m hurdles event at the Irish Life Health Elite Athlete Indoor Micro Meet. Throughout the outdoor 110m Hurdles competitive season Gerard produced gold winning performances from the Control Meeting in Malaga to the City of Lisburn Senior Invitational in Belfast. He retained his Irish title across the 110m Hurdles also. Gerard is making a return to the DNA competition after competing at the 2019 Minsk competition.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Louise Shanahan from Leevale AC coached by Phil O’Dell.
The 800m Olympian debuts the 2022 season for Team Ireland at DNA. After a busy year in 2021 placing within the top 5 across indoor competitions such as the Bryggen Sports Invitational in Manchester’s to the World Athletics Indoor Tour in Spain before her strong performance at the Outdoor 800m Tokyo Olympic Games in July placing 7th within heat 3.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Ruby Millet from St Abbans AC coached by Michael and Eoin Kelly.
The Long jumper who set the U20 National Indoor Record of 6.20 in 2019, is back indoors after her outdoor season in 2021. Last seen indoors in 2020, she was spotted on the podium a number of times from the Irish U20/U23 Indoor Championships where she won silver to winning gold at the Irish Indoor University Championships. 2021 was all outdoors for the long jumper where she had a strong performance at home winning gold at the AAI Games in Morton Stadium before heading to the European U23 Athletics Championships where she finished 12th in the final.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Ciaran Connolly from Le Cheile AC coached by Lisa Dixon.
Throughout the 2020 Indoor Season Ciaran was on the podium for his High Jump performances, such as winning gold at the Irish Indoor University Championships and U20 Indoor Championships.Throughout the 2021 Outdoor High Jump Season Ciaran was taking home first place finishes such as the Northern Ireland Jumps Festival in Belfast and the Irish U23 Championships in Dublin. He will be working hard to bring the success from outdoors to his Indoor season.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### James Kelly from Finn Valley AC coached by John Kelly Sr.
At the 2021 Irish Life Health Indoor Micro Meet James took first place for the shot-put event and a new personal best of 16.72 before heading outdoors for the rest of the 2021 competition calendar, where he also brought home lots of gold from events such as the North Down AC Javelin and Shot-Put Meet in Bangor and the National Athletics League Championships in Manchester.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Catherine McManus from Dublin City Harries AC coached by Brian McManus.
Catherine takes part in another 4x400m Mixed Relay team, after being part of the team that came second at the Irish Life Health Elite Athlete Indoor Micro Meet in Dublin last year in both the 200m and 400m individual competitions. The silver streek continued on the outdoor 400m track at the AAI Games.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Rachel McCann from North Down AC coached by Michael Roberts.
Our second female on the 4x400m Mixed Relay Team was part of the 2021 Irish Championships Outdoor Silver winning Relay Team. Individually Rachel set a new personal best in the 400m outdoor race of 54:12 at the National Athletics League Premier in London where she also won bronze, just under her personal best for the indoor 400m of 55.17 which was set at the 2020 Irish Indoor U20 Championships where she won gold.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Cillin Greene from Galway City Harriers AC coached by Jeremy Lyons and Gerard O’Donnell.
The Olympian was part of the Relay Team that brought Ireland to our first ever relay team to be at an Olympic final in Tokyo 2021 and break the National Record by 4 seconds, with a final time of 3:12.88. Cillin won his first senior outdoor title in 400m event during the National Championsips in 2021.He will form an integral part to this Mixed Relay team.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Robert McDonnell from Galway City Harriers AC coached by Brendan Glynn.
Forming the other half to the Galway City Harriers duo in this 4x400m Relay Team, Robert also went to the Tokyo Olympic Games as part of the Mixed 4x400m relay panel. In 2020 at just 17 Robert came first in both the indoor league and outdoor Irish U20 Championships in the 400m distance. Throughout 2021 he maintained his performance on the outdoor track coming first at the City of Lisburn Senior Invitational in Belfast and second at the Belfast Milers Meet where he ran a personal best time of 46.59. He also had a strong performance at the 2021 U20 European Athletics Championships in the 200m event coming 5th in the final race with a time of 21.18.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Alanna Lally from UCD AC coached by James Nolan.
The 800m Hunt Relay runner has been busy at state side competitions pulling out top 10 performances throughout 2021. In April 2021 she set a new 800m outdoor personal best of 2.04.62 at the North Florida Invitational with her indoor personal best of 2.06.00 set in 2018 at home in Dublin up for review this season.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Jack Raftery from Donore Harriers AC coached by Jeremy Lyons, Gerard O’Donnell and Aideen Sinnott.
The 600m Hunt Relay Runner has been putting in strong performance throughout 2021, being part of the first place finishing outdoor Irish U23 Championship 4x400m mixed relay team. At the 2020 U20 Indoor Championships in Athlone Jack came first with an indoor personal best time of 48.87.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Roisin Harrison from Emerald AC coached by Eoghan McNamara.
The 400m Hunt Relay Runner took top spot on the podium during the outdoor Scottish Joint League Meeting in Glasgow in 2021 with a time of 55.04 an outdoor personal best for Roisin. Her indoor 400m personal best was also set in Glasgow during the 2020 season clocking in at 56.44.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Eanna Madden from Carrick on Shannon AC coached by Jeremy Lyons & Gerard O’Donnell.
The 200m Hunt Relay Runner has had a competitive outdoor 200m season in 2021 winning silver at the Flanders Cup in Belgium and at the Athletics Northern Ireland Open in Belfast. This is sure to prove a strong basis for his performance at DNA cheered on by coach and teammate Gerard O’Donnell.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Sarah McCarthy from Mid-Sutton AC coached by Sandra Daly.
Competing in the 2x200m Mixed Relay event, Sarah has had a strong start to the indoor season, placing 6th at the Lee Valley new Year Open in London before coming first at the AAI National Indoor league Round 1 in a time of 24.14. At the same competition Sarah set a new personal best time in the 60m race at 7.57. In 2021 Sarah came second at the Meeting National de la Roche sur Yon in France during the outdoor 200m event in a time of 23.53 a new personal best for Sarah.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Mark Smyth from Raheny Shamrock AC coached by Kay Bannon.
Joining Sarah in the 2x200m Mixed Relay, Mark is also looking to build on his strong start this indoor season, he finished first at the AAI Indoor League Round 1 200m race with a time of 21.33, just off his personal best time of 21.04. Throughout the indoor 2020 season Mark brought home gold to Raheny from the Irish U23, University and National Indoor Championships. Mark broke the 21 second barrier for the first tme in 2021 with his outdoor PB of 20.91.

dublincityharriers19w
It is with a heavy heart that we share the news of the passing of our esteemed club coach, stalwart, and friend, Brian McManus, who was laid to rest last week.
Brian leaves behind an extraordinary legacy within the athletics community, beautifully captured in this tribute by Dermot Nagle on behalf of the members of Dublin City Harriers and Celtic DCH last week:
“We are heartbroken saying goodbye to our esteemed club member, Brian McManus.
It’s probably a little known fact but Brian was the grandson of the legendary Donore Harrier, Charlie McManus. Athletics was in his blood but it was Dublin City Harriers which he joined to hone his sprinting skills, which were considerable.
He quickly established himself as an accomplished athlete and was a member of some great DCH teams of the 1970s and 1980’s. Brian was an international athlete at both junior and senior levels at 400m and 4 x 400m, in which he recorded sub 48 secs, more than 40 years ago.
Following retirement Brian was involved in administration and was club secretary for a period. It was really coaching which he preferred and over time he put together a strong group of athletes who achieved much. All of Brian’s considerable talents were available to and used by DCH. His quiet, modest, and relaxed approach hid a steely determination to achieve pre-set aims and ambitions.
Above all Brian was a family man; he adored Mary and his daughters Susan and Catherine all of whom were international athletes and represented our country with distinction.
Tomorrow, young and old, we will form a tearful guard of honour at the church. We will mourn and miss this fabulous man, our colleague, our clubmate and our friend who was taken from us too soon, far too soon”.
Rest in peace, Brian. You will be deeply and sadly missed, but your legacy will live on in every lap we run.
bassless19w
So sorry to hear this. He was an absolute gent.

Title: Celtic/DCH Athletics Club on Instagram: "It is with a heavy heart that we share the news of the passing of our esteemed club coach, stalwart, and friend, Brian McManus, who was laid to rest last week. 

Brian leaves behind an extraordinary legacy within the athletics community, beautifully captured in this tribute by Dermot Nagle on behalf of the members of Dublin City Harriers and Celtic DCH last week:

“We are heartbroken saying goodbye to our esteemed club member, Brian McManus.

It’s probably a little known fact but Brian was the grandson of the legendary Donore Harrier, Charlie McManus. Athletics was in his blood but it was Dublin City Harriers which he joined to hone his sprinting skills, which were considerable.

He quickly established himself as an accomplished athlete and was a member of some great DCH teams of the 1970s and 1980’s. Brian was an international athlete at both junior and senior levels at 400m and 4 x 400m, in which he recorded sub 48 secs, more than 40 years ago.

Following retirement Brian was involved in administration and was club secretary for a period. It was really coaching which he preferred and over time he put together a strong group of athletes who achieved much. All of Brian’s considerable talents were available to and used by DCH. His quiet, modest, and relaxed approach hid a steely determination to achieve pre-set aims and ambitions.

Above all Brian was a family man; he adored Mary and his daughters Susan and Catherine all of whom were international athletes and represented our country with distinction.

Tomorrow, young and old, we will form a tearful guard of honour at the church. We will mourn and miss this fabulous man, our colleague, our clubmate and our friend who was taken from us too soon, far too soon”.

Rest in peace, Brian. You will be deeply and sadly missed, but your legacy will live on in every lap we run."

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Gerard O’Donnell from Carrick on Shannon AC coached by Jeremy Lyons and Aideen Sinnott.
The Athletics Ireland RDO is back in action for the 2022 season, the limited competitive season in 2021 seen him still have a very strong performance coming first in the 60m hurdles event at the Irish Life Health Elite Athlete Indoor Micro Meet. Throughout the outdoor 110m Hurdles competitive season Gerard produced gold winning performances from the Control Meeting in Malaga to the City of Lisburn Senior Invitational in Belfast. He retained his Irish title across the 110m Hurdles also. Gerard is making a return to the DNA competition after competing at the 2019 Minsk competition.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Louise Shanahan from Leevale AC coached by Phil O’Dell.
The 800m Olympian debuts the 2022 season for Team Ireland at DNA. After a busy year in 2021 placing within the top 5 across indoor competitions such as the Bryggen Sports Invitational in Manchester’s to the World Athletics Indoor Tour in Spain before her strong performance at the Outdoor 800m Tokyo Olympic Games in July placing 7th within heat 3.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Ruby Millet from St Abbans AC coached by Michael and Eoin Kelly.
The Long jumper who set the U20 National Indoor Record of 6.20 in 2019, is back indoors after her outdoor season in 2021. Last seen indoors in 2020, she was spotted on the podium a number of times from the Irish U20/U23 Indoor Championships where she won silver to winning gold at the Irish Indoor University Championships. 2021 was all outdoors for the long jumper where she had a strong performance at home winning gold at the AAI Games in Morton Stadium before heading to the European U23 Athletics Championships where she finished 12th in the final.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Ciaran Connolly from Le Cheile AC coached by Lisa Dixon.
Throughout the 2020 Indoor Season Ciaran was on the podium for his High Jump performances, such as winning gold at the Irish Indoor University Championships and U20 Indoor Championships.Throughout the 2021 Outdoor High Jump Season Ciaran was taking home first place finishes such as the Northern Ireland Jumps Festival in Belfast and the Irish U23 Championships in Dublin. He will be working hard to bring the success from outdoors to his Indoor season.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### James Kelly from Finn Valley AC coached by John Kelly Sr.
At the 2021 Irish Life Health Indoor Micro Meet James took first place for the shot-put event and a new personal best of 16.72 before heading outdoors for the rest of the 2021 competition calendar, where he also brought home lots of gold from events such as the North Down AC Javelin and Shot-Put Meet in Bangor and the National Athletics League Championships in Manchester.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Catherine McManus from Dublin City Harries AC coached by Brian McManus.
Catherine takes part in another 4x400m Mixed Relay team, after being part of the team that came second at the Irish Life Health Elite Athlete Indoor Micro Meet in Dublin last year in both the 200m and 400m individual competitions. The silver streek continued on the outdoor 400m track at the AAI Games.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Rachel McCann from North Down AC coached by Michael Roberts.
Our second female on the 4x400m Mixed Relay Team was part of the 2021 Irish Championships Outdoor Silver winning Relay Team. Individually Rachel set a new personal best in the 400m outdoor race of 54:12 at the National Athletics League Premier in London where she also won bronze, just under her personal best for the indoor 400m of 55.17 which was set at the 2020 Irish Indoor U20 Championships where she won gold.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Cillin Greene from Galway City Harriers AC coached by Jeremy Lyons and Gerard O’Donnell.
The Olympian was part of the Relay Team that brought Ireland to our first ever relay team to be at an Olympic final in Tokyo 2021 and break the National Record by 4 seconds, with a final time of 3:12.88. Cillin won his first senior outdoor title in 400m event during the National Championsips in 2021.He will form an integral part to this Mixed Relay team.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Robert McDonnell from Galway City Harriers AC coached by Brendan Glynn.
Forming the other half to the Galway City Harriers duo in this 4x400m Relay Team, Robert also went to the Tokyo Olympic Games as part of the Mixed 4x400m relay panel. In 2020 at just 17 Robert came first in both the indoor league and outdoor Irish U20 Championships in the 400m distance. Throughout 2021 he maintained his performance on the outdoor track coming first at the City of Lisburn Senior Invitational in Belfast and second at the Belfast Milers Meet where he ran a personal best time of 46.59. He also had a strong performance at the 2021 U20 European Athletics Championships in the 200m event coming 5th in the final race with a time of 21.18.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Alanna Lally from UCD AC coached by James Nolan.
The 800m Hunt Relay runner has been busy at state side competitions pulling out top 10 performances throughout 2021. In April 2021 she set a new 800m outdoor personal best of 2.04.62 at the North Florida Invitational with her indoor personal best of 2.06.00 set in 2018 at home in Dublin up for review this season.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Jack Raftery from Donore Harriers AC coached by Jeremy Lyons, Gerard O’Donnell and Aideen Sinnott.
The 600m Hunt Relay Runner has been putting in strong performance throughout 2021, being part of the first place finishing outdoor Irish U23 Championship 4x400m mixed relay team. At the 2020 U20 Indoor Championships in Athlone Jack came first with an indoor personal best time of 48.87.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Roisin Harrison from Emerald AC coached by Eoghan McNamara.
The 400m Hunt Relay Runner took top spot on the podium during the outdoor Scottish Joint League Meeting in Glasgow in 2021 with a time of 55.04 an outdoor personal best for Roisin. Her indoor 400m personal best was also set in Glasgow during the 2020 season clocking in at 56.44.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Eanna Madden from Carrick on Shannon AC coached by Jeremy Lyons & Gerard O’Donnell.
The 200m Hunt Relay Runner has had a competitive outdoor 200m season in 2021 winning silver at the Flanders Cup in Belgium and at the Athletics Northern Ireland Open in Belfast. This is sure to prove a strong basis for his performance at DNA cheered on by coach and teammate Gerard O’Donnell.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Sarah McCarthy from Mid-Sutton AC coached by Sandra Daly.
Competing in the 2x200m Mixed Relay event, Sarah has had a strong start to the indoor season, placing 6th at the Lee Valley new Year Open in London before coming first at the AAI National Indoor league Round 1 in a time of 24.14. At the same competition Sarah set a new personal best time in the 60m race at 7.57. In 2021 Sarah came second at the Meeting National de la Roche sur Yon in France during the outdoor 200m event in a time of 23.53 a new personal best for Sarah.

# DNA Team Ireland Selection - Athletics Ireland
## Team Ireland:
### Mark Smyth from Raheny Shamrock AC coached by Kay Bannon.
Joining Sarah in the 2x200m Mixed Relay, Mark is also looking to build on his strong start this indoor season, he finished first at the AAI Indoor League Round 1 200m race with a time of 21.33, just off his personal best time of 21.04. Throughout the indoor 2020 season Mark brought home gold to Raheny from the Irish U23, University and National Indoor Championships. Mark broke the 21 second barrier for the first tme in 2021 with his outdoor PB of 20.91.

# Dooney Family Join Prestigious List - Athletics Ireland
## Dooney Family Join Prestigious List
#### Dooney Family Become the 13th Father and Son to be Capped for Ireland at Senior Level
*Information compiled by Pierce O’Callaghan
Following on from Tuesday’s announcement that Conor Dooney (Raheny Shamrock AC) will now represent Ireland at the European Cross Country Championships in Bulgaria, the Dooney family have made a bit of history of their own. Conor’s father Roy Dooney was capped 19 times for Ireland at senior level. Together they become the 13th father and son to be capped for Ireland at senior level since 1876. Making it a real family affair younger brother Kevin will also be in the team representing Ireland in the U23 race in Bulgaria.

# Dooney Family Join Prestigious List - Athletics Ireland
## Dooney Family Join Prestigious List
#### Previous Father and Son Caps
The previous time this happened was earlier in the year with Eamon and John Coghlan when John gained his first cap at the Penn Relays in April. They join current father & son combinations of Tim & Timmy Crowe, Brendan & Shane Quinn, Paul & Colin Quirke.
Sara Treacy is the daughter of Siobhan Lonergan who was capped four times for Ireland at senior level. Linked to this is the mother & son combination of Patricia Amond & Marcus Lawler and the father, mother and daughter combination of Brian McManus, Mary McManus (nee McKenna) and their daughter Catherine who won her first cap at the European Team Championships in June 2014. In addition to this the father & daughter combination of Mark & Katie Kirk who became the first father & daughter to win Irish senior titles since the championships began in 1873.

Title: Fast Runner: Kevin Dooney
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8
**Kevin Dooney, son of Roy and Greta and brother of Conor, comes from a family of Irish international athletes.**
A product of the American collegiate system, the 24-year-old recently represented Ireland at the European Cross Country Championships in December 2017.
For the year ahead, the Raheny Shamrock runner has ambitions of qualifying for the World Half Marathon Championships and the European Athletics Championships, as well as running a personal best on the track.
Additionally, Dooney will look to increase his mileage in 2018 as he considers a marathon debut in the future.
**Profile**
Name: Kevin Dooney
Age (Jan 2018): 24
Hometown: Dublin, Ireland
Club: Raheny Shamrock AC
Main disciplines: 10,000m & Half Marathon
Other disciplines/events: 5,000m & cross country
Full-time athlete/work/studying: Civil servant working fulltime in the Department of Communications, Climate Action and Environment
**Goals or targets for 2018**
1) Qualify for the World Half Marathon Championships in Valencia in March

 2) Qualify for European Athletics Championships in Berlin in August

 3) Consistently build up to higher mileage with an eye to a marathon debut in the coming years

 4) Run a PB on the track, my current ones have stood since 2014 so I think it’s time they were rewritten
**Career Highlights**
1) Winning two national titles (10,000m/ half marathon) in three weeks over the summer

 2) My first senior international cap at the European Cross Country, 2016

 3) Winning Penn Relays College Championship 5,000m in 2014
**Personal bests**
1) Half-marathon: 66:05

 2) 10,000m: 29:10

 3) 5,000m: 13:59

#### **Interesting or fun facts**
I studied history at Yale University in America and also captained the cross country team in my senior year.
In getting my first senior cap for Ireland, I completed the family set of my father, mother and two brothers being internationals.
Until April 2017, I timed all my runs on the same €10 Casio watch. I eventually caved to the Garmin peer pressure and haven’t looked back. Everything I do now gets logged on Strava despite my coach wondering who could possibly care or want to see what sessions I do.

#### **Why do you run?**
I try not to question that too much. It’s just what I do and how I see myself now. It is a brutal sport so I see no point in going after it half-heartedly and getting half-hearted results. I’ve been lucky enough to be successful throughout my career, which has kept me wanting to come back for more.

#### **Favourite training session**
Mile repeats with 60 seconds recovery. This was a staple workout in college, generally, we would do seven and it was a very useful benchmark of where I was fitness wise.

#### **Least favourite training session**
3 x mile at 5k race pace followed by 2-3 x 400m. Just a painful session. I only ever did it twice, but it still stands out as the one I remember hurting the most.

#### **Favourite pre-race food**
I’ve been eating a banana and three fig rolls before every race since I was 14, hasn’t let me down yet.

#### **Favourite post-race food**
I generally race on a Sunday and so head back to the parent’s house for the Sunday roast, and it’s always a highly satisfying feed prepared by my dad.

#### **Favourite runner or runners**
It has been great to see the current group of younger British athletes running so well and competing on the world stage.
Historically I’ve always looked at the Irish marathon runners of the 1980’s and 90’s and hope to reach a similar level.

#### **Chosen charity for ‘fast runners: class of 2018’**
Aware, which is a depression & bipolar disorder charity in Ireland.
_More information about the group of ‘fast runners: class of 2018’ can be found here._

Source: https://stonybrookathletics.com/news/2019/11/1/womens-cross-country-a-family-affair-o-reilly-readies-for-america-east-championship
Title: A Family Affair: O’Reilly Readies for America East Championship
Chunks: 0,1,2
**STONY BROOK, N.Y.**– Picture this: An Irish family of 10, all runners, competing on a reality television show to find Ireland's most fit family. Seems like a scenario straight out of a work of fiction but nonetheless was real life for senior Clodagh O'Reilly**(Cavan, Ireland)**and her family back in 2013.
The O'Reillys graced the television screen as part of a program called "Ireland's Fittest Family," a show that pits families against each other in fitness competitions to decide who is Ireland's most athletic family. The O'Reilly family was featured on the show's very first season and as fate would have it, they won the whole thing.
"There were 12 families on the show so each week they would knock a family out," O'Reilly said. "It was interesting because there were families from every sports background: Gaelic football, MMA fighters, runners, people who were into gymnastics and we won the whole show. It was back in 2013 and it's still going, so that's one of my claims to fame."
Clodagh and her siblings' running DNA can be traced back to her parents who both ran in college back home in Ireland and met at a track meet. The rest is history as each of the O'Reilly children took up the sport growing up. As the sixth child out of eight siblings, O'Reilly differed from the rest of her family as she was the sole one to take the leap of faith and come to the United States to run collegiately. Thus, bringing her to Long Island.
"I had no idea about the level of sport here and the level of collegiate athletics because we don't have it at home in Ireland," O'Reilly mentioned. "I was just completely overwhelmed by the high standard and the support they get at an institution like this. There's nothing like this at home, so once I saw this I said 'I have to have it.' It would have been silly to give up an opportunity as amazing as this. I'm very glad I'm here, I'm glad I chose Stony Brook."
With her family's support behind her, O'Reilly landed in New York in 2016 for her freshman season and much like any new kid on campus, she experienced some bumps in the road as she was acclimating to her new surroundings while balancing the demands of being a student-athlete.

"Definitely the transition of high school to college and add on top of that athletics and moving to a new country was a lot," O'Reilly stated. "So getting used to the time management of all of it and trying to balance everything definitely was like a juggling act. Then, I was injured my freshman year during second semester so I was out for all of outdoor track."
Despite the rollercoaster of a rookie season, O'Reilly has no regrets and credits the second family she found within her team with shaping her to the person she is today.
"The people in my locker room, the people in the boys' locker room and everyone who's part of our team is the reason I'm happy here," O'Reilly exclaimed."They are my second family."
This Saturday, O'Reilly and her family are set to delve back into competitive action, however it won't be with her hereditary family back home in Ireland on a reality television show. This time it'll be with her Seawolves family at the America East Championship.
Looking back at the squad's body of work this year, the expectations for this championship weekend have drastically shifted from where they were originally during the preseason.
"When I thought about conference back in the preseason in August, I thought we only had an outside shot of a conference title this year," O'Reilly said. "But this week looking into conference, I think we have a legitimate chance. I've been so impressed by the performance of our entire team this semester, I feel like everyone's worked very hard and everyone's really stepped up. Everyone in the locker room has worked so hard all summer long, putting their summer training in, running all their miles, and it's really shown this season because we've been racing exceptionally well in comparison to other years."
"The goal and the focus is definitely on our team and race-wise I want to make sure that Holly (Manning) and Tara (Hauff), who I've been training with all season, are right there with me. We're going to work as a team and individually I'm going to do whatever I can to put us in the best position we can be in."
**Coach Ronan on the championship weekend:**

"Our women's team, led by Clodagh O Reilly, Holly Manning and Tara Hauff, has gradually worked their way into the conversation for the conference title that we compete for on Saturday. Now they understand that the team has to produce the best run of the season so far to contend with New Hampshire and Vermont to achieve the win. But there is a competitive spirit running through this group that I feel will make the other teams have to be at their best to hold them off in the later stages of the race."

# Dooney Family Join Prestigious List - Athletics Ireland
## Dooney Family Join Prestigious List
#### Dooney Family Become the 13th Father and Son to be Capped for Ireland at Senior Level
*Information compiled by Pierce O’Callaghan
Following on from Tuesday’s announcement that Conor Dooney (Raheny Shamrock AC) will now represent Ireland at the European Cross Country Championships in Bulgaria, the Dooney family have made a bit of history of their own. Conor’s father Roy Dooney was capped 19 times for Ireland at senior level. Together they become the 13th father and son to be capped for Ireland at senior level since 1876. Making it a real family affair younger brother Kevin will also be in the team representing Ireland in the U23 race in Bulgaria.

# Dooney Family Join Prestigious List - Athletics Ireland
## Dooney Family Join Prestigious List
#### Previous Father and Son Caps
The previous time this happened was earlier in the year with Eamon and John Coghlan when John gained his first cap at the Penn Relays in April. They join current father & son combinations of Tim & Timmy Crowe, Brendan & Shane Quinn, Paul & Colin Quirke.
Sara Treacy is the daughter of Siobhan Lonergan who was capped four times for Ireland at senior level. Linked to this is the mother & son combination of Patricia Amond & Marcus Lawler and the father, mother and daughter combination of Brian McManus, Mary McManus (nee McKenna) and their daughter Catherine who won her first cap at the European Team Championships in June 2014. In addition to this the father & daughter combination of Mark & Katie Kirk who became the first father & daughter to win Irish senior titles since the championships began in 1873.

**Kevin Dooney, son of Roy and Greta and brother of Conor, comes from a family of Irish international athletes.**
A product of the American collegiate system, the 24-year-old recently represented Ireland at the European Cross Country Championships in December 2017.
For the year ahead, the Raheny Shamrock runner has ambitions of qualifying for the World Half Marathon Championships and the European Athletics Championships, as well as running a personal best on the track.
Additionally, Dooney will look to increase his mileage in 2018 as he considers a marathon debut in the future.
**Profile**
Name: Kevin Dooney
Age (Jan 2018): 24
Hometown: Dublin, Ireland
Club: Raheny Shamrock AC
Main disciplines: 10,000m & Half Marathon
Other disciplines/events: 5,000m & cross country
Full-time athlete/work/studying: Civil servant working fulltime in the Department of Communications, Climate Action and Environment
**Goals or targets for 2018**
1) Qualify for the World Half Marathon Championships in Valencia in March

 2) Qualify for European Athletics Championships in Berlin in August

 3) Consistently build up to higher mileage with an eye to a marathon debut in the coming years

 4) Run a PB on the track, my current ones have stood since 2014 so I think it’s time they were rewritten
**Career Highlights**
1) Winning two national titles (10,000m/ half marathon) in three weeks over the summer

 2) My first senior international cap at the European Cross Country, 2016

 3) Winning Penn Relays College Championship 5,000m in 2014
**Personal bests**
1) Half-marathon: 66:05

 2) 10,000m: 29:10

 3) 5,000m: 13:59
texts.1:
#### **Interesting or fun facts**
I studied history at Yale University in America and also captained the cross country team in my senior year.
In getting my first senior cap for Ireland, I completed the family set of my father, mother and two brothers being internationals.
Until April 2017, I timed all my runs on the same €10 Casio watch. I eventually caved to the Garmin peer pressure and haven’t looked back. Everything I do now gets logged on Strava despite my coach wondering who could possibly care or want to see what sessions I do.
texts.2:
#### **Why do you run?**
I try not to question that too much. It’s just what I do and how I see myself now. It is a brutal sport so I see no point in going after it half-heartedly and getting half-hearted results. I’ve been lucky enough to be successful throughout my career, which has kept me wanting to come back for more.
texts.3:
#### **Favourite training session**
Mile repeats with 60 seconds recovery. This was a staple workout in college, generally, we would do seven and it was a very useful benchmark of where I was fitness wise.
texts.4:
#### **Least favourite training session**
3 x mile at 5k race pace followed by 2-3 x 400m. Just a painful session. I only ever did it twice, but it still stands out as the one I remember hurting the most.
texts.5:
#### **Favourite pre-race food**
I’ve been eating a banana and three fig rolls before every race since I was 14, hasn’t let me down yet.
texts.6:
#### **Favourite post-race food**
I generally race on a Sunday and so head back to the parent’s house for the Sunday roast, and it’s always a highly satisfying feed prepared by my dad.
texts.7:
#### **Favourite runner or runners**
It has been great to see the current group of younger British athletes running so well and competing on the world stage.
Historically I’ve always looked at the Irish marathon runners of the 1980’s and 90’s and hope to reach a similar level.
texts.8:
#### **Chosen charity for ‘fast runners: class of 2018’**
Aware, which is a depression & bipolar disorder charity in Ireland.
_More information about the group of ‘fast runners: class of 2018’ can be found here._

**STONY BROOK, N.Y.**– Picture this: An Irish family of 10, all runners, competing on a reality television show to find Ireland's most fit family. Seems like a scenario straight out of a work of fiction but nonetheless was real life for senior Clodagh O'Reilly**(Cavan, Ireland)**and her family back in 2013.
The O'Reillys graced the television screen as part of a program called "Ireland's Fittest Family," a show that pits families against each other in fitness competitions to decide who is Ireland's most athletic family. The O'Reilly family was featured on the show's very first season and as fate would have it, they won the whole thing.
"There were 12 families on the show so each week they would knock a family out," O'Reilly said. "It was interesting because there were families from every sports background: Gaelic football, MMA fighters, runners, people who were into gymnastics and we won the whole show. It was back in 2013 and it's still going, so that's one of my claims to fame."
Clodagh and her siblings' running DNA can be traced back to her parents who both ran in college back home in Ireland and met at a track meet. The rest is history as each of the O'Reilly children took up the sport growing up. As the sixth child out of eight siblings, O'Reilly differed from the rest of her family as she was the sole one to take the leap of faith and come to the United States to run collegiately. Thus, bringing her to Long Island.
"I had no idea about the level of sport here and the level of collegiate athletics because we don't have it at home in Ireland," O'Reilly mentioned. "I was just completely overwhelmed by the high standard and the support they get at an institution like this. There's nothing like this at home, so once I saw this I said 'I have to have it.' It would have been silly to give up an opportunity as amazing as this. I'm very glad I'm here, I'm glad I chose Stony Brook."
With her family's support behind her, O'Reilly landed in New York in 2016 for her freshman season and much like any new kid on campus, she experienced some bumps in the road as she was acclimating to her new surroundings while balancing the demands of being a student-athlete.
texts.1:
"Definitely the transition of high school to college and add on top of that athletics and moving to a new country was a lot," O'Reilly stated. "So getting used to the time management of all of it and trying to balance everything definitely was like a juggling act. Then, I was injured my freshman year during second semester so I was out for all of outdoor track."
Despite the rollercoaster of a rookie season, O'Reilly has no regrets and credits the second family she found within her team with shaping her to the person she is today.
"The people in my locker room, the people in the boys' locker room and everyone who's part of our team is the reason I'm happy here," O'Reilly exclaimed."They are my second family."
This Saturday, O'Reilly and her family are set to delve back into competitive action, however it won't be with her hereditary family back home in Ireland on a reality television show. This time it'll be with her Seawolves family at the America East Championship.
Looking back at the squad's body of work this year, the expectations for this championship weekend have drastically shifted from where they were originally during the preseason.
"When I thought about conference back in the preseason in August, I thought we only had an outside shot of a conference title this year," O'Reilly said. "But this week looking into conference, I think we have a legitimate chance. I've been so impressed by the performance of our entire team this semester, I feel like everyone's worked very hard and everyone's really stepped up. Everyone in the locker room has worked so hard all summer long, putting their summer training in, running all their miles, and it's really shown this season because we've been racing exceptionally well in comparison to other years."
"The goal and the focus is definitely on our team and race-wise I want to make sure that Holly (Manning) and Tara (Hauff), who I've been training with all season, are right there with me. We're going to work as a team and individually I'm going to do whatever I can to put us in the best position we can be in."
**Coach Ronan on the championship weekend:**
texts.2: "Our women's team, led by Clodagh O Reilly, Holly Manning and Tara Hauff, has gradually worked their way into the conversation for the conference title that we compete for on Saturday. Now they understand that the team has to produce the best run of the season so far to contend with New Hampshire and Vermont to achieve the win. But there is a competitive spirit running through this group that I feel will make the other teams have to be at their best to hold them off in the later stages of the race."
